questions.q: Why does inference typically need three separate SLOs — latency, throughput, and availability — instead of one combined 'is it up' target?
options: Because each one can be violated while the other two still look fine, so a single combined metric would hide real problems
Because cloud providers require exactly three SLOs per service by policy
Because latency, throughput, and availability are actually the same measurement under different names
Because a single SLO is technically impossible to configure in any monitoring tool
questions.explain: A service can be fast and under-loaded yet unavailable due to a crash, or available and fast on average yet failing a latency SLO in its tail — the three fail independently.

questions.q: Why is p99 latency, rather than average latency, the metric a tail-latency SLO is usually written against?
options: Average latency is always higher than p99 latency
p99 latency and average latency always move together, so it doesn't matter which is used
Average latency can look fine while a meaningful fraction of callers experience the slowest responses, which an average hides
p99 latency is simpler to calculate than an average
questions.explain: An average can hide a tail-latency problem entirely; p99 latency captures the experience of the slowest 1% of requests, which is where real user pain shows up first.

questions.q: Why should a throughput SLO be defined conditionally on latency, rather than as a standalone 'requests per second' number?
options: A sustained rate achieved only by making every request slower isn't meeting a useful throughput target — it's trading the latency SLO away to hit the throughput number
Throughput cannot be measured on GPU-backed services at all
Latency and throughput are unrelated metrics with no connection
Standalone throughput numbers are always more accurate than conditional ones
questions.explain: A raw req/sec number is meaningless without saying what happens to latency at that load; the real target is the highest sustained rate the service can serve while still meeting its latency SLO.

questions.q: What GPU-specific failure mode does this lesson say a generic 'process is running' health check can miss?
options: A disk running out of space on a stateless web server
A missing TLS certificate on a load balancer
A DNS misconfiguration unrelated to the model at all
An out-of-memory crash or driver fault that keeps the process technically running but the model unable to actually serve requests
questions.explain: A health check that doesn't actually exercise the model can report healthy even when a GPU-specific failure (OOM, driver fault, failed model load) has made the service unable to really serve requests.

questions.q: Why should a latency SLO be measured across scaling events, including cold starts, rather than only in steady state?
options: Cold starts never affect latency on GPU-backed services
A replica that hasn't finished loading model weights into VRAM can take minutes to become ready, producing a real tail-latency spike that a steady-state-only measurement would miss
Scaling events are irrelevant to any SLO
Steady-state measurement is always more representative than any other window
questions.explain: Cold starts on GPU-backed replicas can take minutes, which is exactly the kind of real-world latency spike a steady-state-only SLO measurement would fail to catch.
